utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We'll continue now with the evidence of Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your examination by Mr. Lukic will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth that you make at the outset of the evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On Friday, we finished on the topic of having documents taken away. Does the loss, destruction, or seizure of documents mean loss of any kind of civic status in the FRY at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the loss of any document does not mean the loss of status of a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I've already mentioned, if a passport is lost abroad, there is an appropriate procedure to be applied, and the same goes for things that happen within the country; that is to say, that whoever loses his or her passport is duty-bound to report that to the closest police station. The procedure is fully prescribed. The document is proclaimed invalid and a new document is issued. The same goes for personal identity card. That is also a public document that is used for showing a person's identity or proving a person's identity. As for personal identity cards and passports and other documents, there are registers that are kept. For personal IDs and passports, in addition to registers, there are files as well. There are also IS records; that is, the unified information system. So the details of each and every person are kept in several places. I would particularly like to point out the register. The register registers every passport that is issued, that goes for travel documents and personal IDs. Files of issued passports and IDs are kept in accordance with the alphabetical order or either in the Cyrillic or the Latin alphabet. So we can always establish who this person is. If all documents were lost, we look at the print of the right index finger or also statements can be taken from two witnesses. I would like to note that, in addition to the ministry, records on citizens are kept in other services, too, like the register of birth certificates and the register of citizens. They belong to the ministry of state administration and local administration. So this is an independent ministry that also has the details of all the persons who were born in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, these registers, is there a specific register of a particular ethnic group? For example, is it possible to destroy the register of citizens of Albanian ethnic background or are registers mixed, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a single type of register. I said that documents are registered in the order which they are issued. There is a decree with a very long name on archive materials, and it states -- I can't remember its exact name now, but it states that records have to be kept permanently, that's the way it's been since 1945. I don't know if there are any registers before that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not clear from that answer. Is it possible to destroy the register of citizens of Albanian ethnic background or are registers mixed? The English translation does not make a clear statement in answer to that. Could you answer that again, please, just the simple question whether the registers are kept on an ethnic -- according to ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. There is only a single type of register. There are no registers on the basis of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registers are compiled in the order in which documents are issued and requests received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was done with records just before the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think that these records were relocated, and I think that this was done by employees from the administration of the border police. I think they were relocated from the secretariats because it was assumed that these would be targets of NATO attacks. So this was done with a view to preserving these records. Where it was that they were taken away, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these records were handed over to UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I heard at the administration that this was, indeed, handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the source of your information on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I've already said, in contacts with employees of the administration because that is my own line of work, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, if there's only one record, why give it to UNMIK when it obviously will contain records of people who will no longer be in Kosovo after the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know why this was done; but, as I said, in addition to these registers, all the information is kept in computers as well. According to our system, this is called a databank of persons; that is to say, that there are electronic records of all the persons to who personal identity cards were issued to and who lived in which area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have missed it, but I didn't hear an earlier reference to computers. Are you saying they were computerised records in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, not only in 1999 but also the years before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would also like to clarify something. Is there just one record or several records or several types of books or ledgers where the status of citizens is registered?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the Ministry of the Interior keeps records on personal identity cards that were issued, on passports issued, driver's licences issued, and traffic licences issued; whereas, the Ministry for State Administration is the ministry to which local registry officers belong, and that is where birth certificates are issued and kept and death certificates and all other records pertaining to citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with this particular area, a minor, a person under age, a child of the age of 10, does such a person have a personal ID?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a person does not have an ID and does not have the obligation to have an ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's assume that this person doesn't have a passport, does this person have the status of a citizen and is this person recorded in records; and if so, in what records to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, in the records of birth. Every child that is born has to be registered. Also, there is a register of the population. Parents are duty-bound to register their children at the SUPs, too, so records can be found about them in the SUPs stating that such persons are citizens of a particular town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the record of citizenship, are they registered there, too?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as a child is born, the child is registered in the register of citizenship; although, I would like to say that the rules on registration changed several times in our country. So information on citizenship were sometimes registered in birth registers and sometimes in citizenship registers. But I cannot give you the exact periods of time when the records were kept and in which way; but, at any rate, it was always at the local registry offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, one of these records, the record of births, how many copies exist of each and every one of them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that a register or record of births is kept in a single copy, but the register of citizens in two copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The register of citizens that is kept in two copies is kept in how many places?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Records of citizenship are kept in two different places, primarily at the local register offices; and the second copy of the register of citizens is kept in the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are all of these records kept on a mixed basis, irrespective of the ethnic background of the persons concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All records are kept on the basis of the order in which requests were received; that is to say, once a child is born and once the parents come to register the child, then an entry is made in the book of births and in the book of citizenship. If I'm being clear, all the records are a single one, so to speak, so there is no particular record of different ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard testimony here that in depth, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, personal identity cards were being taken away. We heard stories about border crossings, when people were leaving Kosovo and Metohija, personal IDs were being taken away. Is there any point in that, to take a personal ID card away from a person if one wishes to destroy his identity as a citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view, that is totally pointless. As I've said, in several places, there are records that are kept about each and every citizen. So someone's identity can always be established. I would like to give an example here. Asylum seekers, quite a few citizens of the former SFRY and of the FRY went illegally to Western countries, and then they were deported or re-admitted into our country. As for documents, they didn't have any on them. They gave information; and on the basis of the information they provided, we established that they were our citizens. For those persons who were our citizens, we sent replies to the state organs of the other countries saying that, yes, these were our citizens; and, of course, we have to be prepared to have them re-admitted into the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Ognjenovic testified before you from the Vrbnica border crossing, and he was asked about that, whether personal IDs were taken away at the border crossing. Nebojsa Ognjenovic, as a member of the border police station, as he carries out his duties at work, does he have anything to do whatsoever with personal IDs? Does he ever ask a person who comes to his border crossing to show him his or her personal ID card?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the law on crossing the state border and moving within the border area, the procedure is prescribed in full. Identity of persons is checked in this area and identity is established on the basis of a travel document, or rather, a passport. As I said, there are several types of travel documents in our country, and that's why I use that terminology, but the jargon is invariably passport. In this area, the officials only check whether a person does have a travel document, whether it is that person's travel document, whether it's a valid travel document, and whether the person has a visa for travelling to a particular country that requires a visa; that is to say, they don't ask anyone for a personal ID. A personal ID card is a document that is used internally, only within the country within which it was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If a person would have a regular, valid personal ID card and would show Nebojsa Ognjenovic or one of his colleagues that personal ID card, could he let such a person leave the country on the basis of the personal ID card?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The said person could not leave the country because in order to leave the country one has to have a travel document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Yugoslavia in 1999, were there any international agreements with Albania and Macedonia in place at the time that would have allowed for the movement of citizens across state borders carrying nothing more than an identification document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our country had no such agreements with these countries or at least none that I knew of. Since I had been dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija for that sort of business, I should have been informed by the administration itself of any such agreements that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. This thing is not very clear. Were there cases where people, now before all this crisis, travelled across the border to Albania or other places without a passport on the basis of some other identification material? Did they ever travel like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As far as I know, people couldn't travel to any country with an identification document alone. You could have travelled with a passport or with border passes, which was another type of travel documents, and this applied only to those countries with which our country had an actual agreement on this. A border pass is only used by citizens who live in the border belt and only in order to travel to the neighbouring -- to a neighbouring country. There is an agreement that specifies the distance, normally between 20 and 50 kilometres, and maybe there is a list of particular towns and villages of places to which citizens of one country are entitled to travel by using only those border passes, potential destinations in the other country. There are even special border crossings that are sometimes set up for this sort of transit, low-intensity transit across the border. Whoever is in possession of such a border pass can go to a particular number of places in the other country. If you want a more graphic explanation, let's take the case of Albania. They could have travelled to Kupres, for example, but not Tirana, Tirana being too far away from this border pass; or, for example, Romania, which is something I happen to know more about. This is the country that concerns the work of my secretariat. And on the basis of these border passes, the people could only travel to these neighbouring countries and only to a very limited list of places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have one more question. Now, you talked of the registration of citizens in unique registers, not that they were mixed registers or different registers. But did these registers have a column mentioning about the ethnicity of a person? Was there any indication there where somebody had to show his ethnic background in those registers or in the ID cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whenever there was a request for personal identification documents to be issued, that there was a box that stated a person's ethnicity, but no citizen was under an obligation to have this sort of information recorded. They could have if they had opted to; and, normally, this type of information was something you could always find in the records. None of the state bodies had the power to impose on citizens the obligation to state their ethnicity or their ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to pick up where His Honour left off. On an identification document, is there a special category showing any person's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on personal identification documents. Personal information is all you can find there: One's name, one's father's name, the date of birth, the place of birth, the date the document was issued, the authority that issued the document, and validity or date of expiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about passports, is ethnicity displayed on a passport of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Ethnicity is not indicated on a passport either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you discussed with His Honour Judge Chowhan. You mentioned Romania, you said you knew more about that, the cross-border traffic by citizens. Was there any such agreement in place back in 1999 between the FRY, on the one hand, and Romania, on the other?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it did exist. I can't say when the agreement was reached, but it must have been reached about 30 years ago at least, and the same situation applied to the Republic of Hungary. The Novi Sad secretariat is right on the border. It straddles the border to the Republic of Croatia. So we have such an agreement in place with Croatia, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any such agreement between the FRY and Albania in 1999, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we have now sufficiently clarified this area, and I'd like to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 6D130 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the document now. Let me ask you this first: Who issued this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was issued by the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the header, you see the Federal Ministry of the Interior mentioned there, for their information; secretariat of the interior from 1 to 33, to the chief; all border police stations, to the commander; the MUP staff in Pristina, to the head of staff; and the last name mentioned there is administrations within the police headquarters, police administration, traffic police administration, crime police administration, operations centre, for their information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the location of the HQ, I mean the one mentioned among the addressees, can we actually tell the location in the reporting chain or in the reporting system?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the document, you see that it was sent directly to all the secretariats of the interior and border police stations, because they are the ones receiving the certain kinds of instructions here. And only underneath can you see the headquarters of the interior in Pristina; although, in my opinion, the staff only received this for information purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the head of the MUP staff, was he in a position to issue any instructions to the chief of your -- to the head of your administration in purely professional terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If so, I was certainly not aware of that. I don't think that he was in a position to issue any instructions or orders to the head of my administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could the head of the MUP staff use you as a channel to change any rules or any methods that were in your professional purview?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The head of the MUP staff could not do that through me; however, this document is one of the examples showing that anything concerning the line of work that I was involved in came directly from the Ministry of the Interior and was passed along to lower-level organizational units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Lukic. We seem to be without counsel for Mr. Ojdanic for the moment without any indication of why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know why. I know that some guard came in and talked to him, and there seemed to be something going on over here that required his attention, but I'm not sure what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we were concerned that your client was unrepresented in your absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I went out because I received some information which confused me completely, so probably there was some misunderstanding and I thought it was something. I even don't know what it is about. I received some information that I was called out, so I wanted to check what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose if you give me a confusing enough explanation, it might solve the problem, but that shouldn't happen. If there is a reason why you have to leave the courtroom and leave the accused unrepresented, then you have to draw that to the attention of the Bench, so that we can decide what action to take, whether to permit it or not, whether to adjourn if necessary. So, please, in future, deal with it before leaving the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you if the head of the MUP staff could use you to change any rules or any methods that were part of your professional field of work. My question now is: Could he do it without you, I mean change any rules or work methods, the head of the MUP staff, back in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he couldn't change any rules or methods in a professional sense, because as far as I know he was never involved in this line of work himself; therefore, he could not have changed the rules, could he?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before this time you mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the staff. Were you the superior of those working in the border police stations in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not their superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You, as a member of the staff, were you superior to members of the divisions of the border police in the secretariats of the interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not their superior in any way, nor did I, in fact, interfere with their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to punish any of these persons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have that power.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take any personnel-related decisions regarding persons working in your field in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't take any such decisions because I didn't know all those people, nor did I have those powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first about 1998, the summer of 1998, between July and October. Who was the highest-ranking MUP officer of the Republic of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998, in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija, there were General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic. I can't be more specific than this in terms of saying whether they were always there together at the same time; but as far as I remember, one of them was always in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about 1999, from just before the air-strikes to the end of the war, who was the highest-ranking officer of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia who was staying in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think General Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, which of the two, Djordjevic and Stevanovic, was the higher-ranking officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember their specific ranks. I think they were both generals, maybe lieutenant-general or colonel-general; but I think in terms of his function, General Djordjevic was higher-ranking than the other. He was the head of the public security sector, and under him there were all the different services and all the public security officials. General Stevanovic was assistant minister, which would place him, in my opinion, a single rank in the ladder under General Djordjevic. As far as I'm familiar with the system within the Ministry of the Interior, there's the minister of the interior, the deputy minister of the interior, and then sector heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that Stevanovic was an assistant minister. Did Djordjevic hold a ministerial position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There is only one minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand there's only one minister, but I think you've given us the title assistant minister for Stevanovic. Was Djordjevic an assistant minister or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, was he? Was he not? I really don't know. All I know is he was head of the public security sector. So within the ministry, there is the ministry and two sectors. Based on that, I draw the inference that, under the minister, the only people remaining were the sector heads, and there are a number of assistants who are in charge of certain areas. I did not personally know all the assistant ministers that were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your understanding is an assistant minister comes somewhere lower in the ranks than a head of a sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there a deputy minister in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not as far as I remember. Before that time, it was General Radovan Stojicic, who was deputy minister; and, at the same time, he was working as head of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what had happened to him by 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stojicic, and I can't remember the year, back in 1996 -- but I can't give you the exact year. I simply don't remember. Anyway, he was killed. After that, as far as I know, Mr. Djordjevic was the person who he replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us, where were the offices of the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija? Actually, you've already told us, but could you please repeat it for the sake of the next question.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offices of the MUP staff were in the premises of the SUP in Pristina, in the building where the Ministry of the Interior was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you move after the bombing started?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we moved to a shelter, the shelter of the MUP building in Pristina, and the shelter is in the basement of that very same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the place where you were injured?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, who else was also injured?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Desimir Slovic was also injured, he was a member of the staff; and Dusko Adamovic; Tomislav Blagojevic, also a member of the staff, was injured, but the his injuries were lighter; and an employee of the MUP of Pristina got killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many storeys did that building have?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a three-storey building or a four-storey building, I can't remember exactly now, because the SUP of Pristina used several buildings, three I believe, that were interconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long were you under the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that we were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, that is to say, underneath the surface of the earth?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the same time, was that a shelter from the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The place where you were?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remember the meetings that were held at the staff. Do you remember who it was that you saw there? Which top people of the MUP did you see there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the top people of the MUP, it was the minister who attended these meetings; then General Djordjevic as the head of the public security sector; and then I can't remember now whether it was once or twice that the head of the state security sector came as well; and General Obrad Stevanovic came, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the offices where the staff was. Can you tell us, to the best of your recollection, who sat in which office, if you can just give us a description of that. Whose office was next to whose office?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novica Zdravkovic sat in one office. Opposite his office was my office. Next door to my office was Desimir Slovic 's office. And right next to our offices was a biggish office where Dusko Adamovic and Goran Radosavljevic were. Of course, there was also the office where Mr. Mijatovic was and the office where the head of the staff was, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from these offices, were there any other rooms at the SUP of Pristina that were used by the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't use any other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that to say that all the members of the staff were present on that same floor in those few offices?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were talking about documentation and records. Do you know what a green card is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A green card is a card that is issued to a citizen when he registers at a place outside his official place of residence. I can give you an example. If someone lives in Nis, for example, and comes to Novi Sad to study, for instance, or to take care of some work, he is duty-bound to register and that is when he is issued with a green card; that is to say, that he is temporarily residing outside his place of permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would that also apply to someone from Nis who went to study in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That applies to all citizens, regardless of what town they go to. As soon as a person, or rather, a citizen leaves his place of residence, he is duty-bound to register his temporary place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this green card issued -- or rather, was an attempt made to regulate records of citizens in Kosovo and Metohija during the war? I'm sorry. I'm sorry. By then you had already left. I've gone a bit too far. So you don't really know that. Was such a green card issued to Serbs who had left Kosovo and Metohija after the withdrawal of the Serb forces from Kosovo and Metohija, when they withdrew into the interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were issued with these green cards. Too. That is regulated by the Law on the Residence and Domicile of Citizens. Lest there be any confusion, this applies to all citizens of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you something about the border belt. What is the role of the Ministry of the Interior in the border belt?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior issues permits for moving and residing in the border belt, and it issues permits for building facilities in the border belt. In addition to that, the Ministry of the Interior checks movement within the border belt but only in urban areas. Outside the urban areas it is the Army of Yugoslavia that is in charge of such checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the width of the border belt was in 1998 and what the width was in the beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law prescribes that the width of the border belt on land is 100 metres from the borderline. This applies to rivers and lakes, too; however, in the sea, it is two nautical miles. I cannot remember the exact year, but I think that this width was extended to five kilometres, and I think that, just before the bombing started, it was extended to ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier on, we talked about the decision on the establishment of the staff dated the 16th of June, 1999 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1505 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I inquire, it comes on the transcript as June 1999. I think that was June 16th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the document in front of you, Mr. Vucurevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the context of the document any longer. I'm going toll ask you whether you ever received this decision on the establishment of the staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having received such a decision. The only decision that I received and signed was the decision on my own appointment to go out and implement these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any other decision, because we saw that there were some decisions that were passed before this and while you were in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember having received any such decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have in e-court P1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 1, it says that Mr. Sreten Lukic took the floor, and I asked you about this one particular sentence. I know that we even joked about that, since you remembered this particular detail. On page -- or rather, in the sixth line from the bottom, there is a sentence stating: "The elaborated plan of the public security sector with a view to preventing and disabling the entry of the military forces of NATO into our territory." I'm going to ask you something, first of all. The public security sector, is it in charge of defending the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the public security sector is not in charge of defending the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, does the public security sector have the strength and ability to defend the state border?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they do not have the ability to do that because the employees of the Ministry of the Interior, as far as I know, are equipped with light weaponry only.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what's this all about then? What did this sentence mean, this sentence of Sreten Lukic's? What is this that they had conceived in the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this has to do with the following: The barrier should be brought down at the state borders; that is to say, that the state border would be closed. If someone would cross the border individually, then that would be an illegal entry. If someone would do this in an organized manner with military force, barging through that military crossing, then that would be considered an act of aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the proofing, I showed you a document that is not part of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move from this document, the earlier part, Mr. Lukic, which is talking about the service and its work, what is that a reference to? "The service has increased its activities in towns. The annual meetings, headed by the head of staff and the deputy head of staff, were devoted to last year's work. The service has particularly stepped-up its activities towards the borders with Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro in order to thwart terrorists from entering the country." What's the service that's being referred to there? I can't see the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, when they use the word "service" at these meetings, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they say "service," they mean the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're clear about the meaning of the part before the reference to the plan that you've just dealt with, where it says: "The service has particularly stepped-up its activities towards the borders with Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro in order to thwart terrorists from entering the country, prevent weapons, ammunition and other goods from being smuggled and sold on black markets"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I find that clear. I think this is in reference to members of the entire service. Everyone was involved in cutting or disrupting those illegal channels. As I have said, the Ministry of the Interior runs checks along the border, the border crossings, the settlements that straddle the border, and all roads leading to the border. This is the task of the police, the general police unit and the traffic police, as well as those employees whose duty it is to work in the border stations. They check any persons crossing the border, approaching the border, or leaving the border. If someone came to the border and was not carrying weapons or any other illegal goods, we could still stop him after the border crossing itself, and we had the power to check this person and inspect whatever the person was carrying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's immediately after that that Mr. Lukic is recorded as saying: "A plan of the public security department has been worked out to prevent and thwart entry of NATO troops in our territory." The same word "thwart" is used in relation to NATO troops as was used in relation to terrorists. And you say that that cunning plan was to put down the barriers at the border? Are you serious about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I didn't see that plan myself. What I'm giving you is my opinion as to what that could mean. At the meeting itself, I don't remember that this was something that was elaborated on in terms of what the plan actually implied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how relevant this is at this point in time, but was it me who asked you, Mr. Vucurevic, whether you meant this in all earnestness when you told me this about preventing NATO from getting in, something that was to be done by the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was simply something that was supposed to show that someone was illegally entering the country. Take a border crossing, I'm not sure what the strength of that unit might be, but between ten and 20 police officers, let's say, they're hardly in a position to stop anyone forcing their way into a country, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was about to introduce a document that's not part of our case. This is an overview of the interesting security-related information dated the 1st of March, 1999. This was put together by the staff. Let me ask you this: Were any attempts made to cross the border with no travel documents during the presence of the Kosovo Verification Mission monitors in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was an attempt like that that was made at the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing, I think. This is a border crossing that faces the Republic of Macedonia. I can't remember how many citizens were involved. At any rate, they wanted to leave FRY territory without appropriate travel documents. I remember that at the time we got in touch with the High Commissioner for Refugees. As far as I remember, they offered certain guarantees for those people, saying that they would get them across the border without appropriate travel documents, but we put a stop to that simply because it took no more than a couple of days to get those documents issued in a regular procedure. We said that all those citizens should go back to their own local register offices, have proper documents issued, and that they would then be free to leave the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P1224.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see that document, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document that the OTP are likely to be using in their cross-examination. You'll probably be returning to this document, but let me ask you this: What sort of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that this is an overview of the numerical strength of the police in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. The date is the 16th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the Republic of Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What sort of a table is this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an overview of the organizational units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija. What we see here is an overview of all the secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija. If you look at this, you see that there is no other organizational unit aside from the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, we can also see the police stations, can't we?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a full list of all the police stations that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the organizational units in Kosovo and Metohija, that would be a fair summary, wouldn't it? Well then, there was something else that you mentioned that we need to go back to. This is an official chart or overview that was put together in October 1998. If we look at it, do we see the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija in it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No indication of the MUP staff in this chart, which means that it wasn't there as an organizational unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Sreten Lukic or anyone else from the Ministry of the Interior, did any of those people ever tell you that there was a plan to expel ethnic Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked with Sreten Lukic, didn't you? What sort of a leader is he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a true professional. He is strict but unbiased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he tolerate any sort of illegal behaviour by any of the MUP members?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He had no tolerance for that sort of thing. As far as I remember, there were daily reports that were produced; and whenever there were police officers who were suspected of having committed crimes, criminal complaints were filed and disciplinary procedures were instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vucurevic. At this point in time, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic. I have a number of questions for you on behalf of Mr. Nikola Sainovic's Defence. Last Friday, you testified that on the 22nd of July, 1998, you attended a meeting that was also attended by General Djordjevic and General Stevanovic, a meeting that was also attended by members of the MUP staff, as well as the heads of the secretariat in Kosovo. You say that you attended that meeting, too. What I want to know is this: At that meeting, did any of those present mention the need to set up some sort of a Joint Command or, indeed, that such a body had been set up for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anyone mentioning a body like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was this perhaps something that General Djordjevic or General Stevanovic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Generals Djordjevic and Stevanovic, did they perhaps inform those present that Nikola Sainovic was now the commander of this sort of Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no, they never informed anyone of anything like that or anything about Mr. Sainovic being the commander of such a command. I don't remember them mentioning his name at all, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in Kosovo between March 1998 and March 1999. Throughout that time over that year, did you see any document or any order displaying the header of: Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I never set eyes on any document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about during your time in Kosovo, did you receive any order, any sort of instruction from a body called the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my area, I never received any orders or instructions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure when you normally break. Is it 10.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vucurevic. My name is John Ackerman. I'm the counsel for General Pavkovic here, and I have some questions for you just because I have become confused about some things that not only you have testified about but that some of your predecessor witnesses have testified about. And I'm going to at least make a stab at trying to clear up some of my own confusion about some things that I've heard. Okay?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, it is my understanding, and I'm pretty sure that I'm right about this, that you left the MUP staff in Kosovo in late March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The 29th of March, to be more specific; 1999, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were there for like five days of the NATO bombing and then gone?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever return and visit there during the subsequent NATO bombing period?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us, at the beginning of your testimony, that you're a lawyer, so we have that in common. I think one of the things that you and I both know about large organizations, like police and military, is about all of the reporting and paperwork that goes on, and there's lots of it, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but everyone knew only about what they were doing. For security reasons, it was part of the general security culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course. This paper that we have seen a lot of through the course of this trial is used to -- for a couple of purposes at least; to communicate and to create permanent records of events that were occurring during the time. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure I understand your question, sir, or rather, the statement that you are putting to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there are at least two kinds of documents, at least I am familiar with. There are those that are intended to communicate between individuals and organizations, and there are those that are designed to maintain a record, daily record, weekly record, a monthly record of events going on within organizations. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And certainly, especially as a lawyer, you would agree that accuracy in those communications and those records is highly important?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, just from watching you here, I'm convinced that you were very careful yourself to make sure that any records or communications you authored were as accurate as they would possibly be, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I suspect you would say that was also true of your colleagues who you worked with during your stint on the MUP staff and otherwise?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they did the same sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You looked a few moments ago at a document 6D130, and I'd like that brought back up again because there are a couple of questions I want to ask you about it. What I'm interested in is right underneath the date. It shows the organizations to whom this was sent. You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, for instance, there's an indication it was sent to the Federal Ministry of the Interior, SMUP; and after that, there's the designation "for your information," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then if you go down toward the bottom, there's an indication that it's going to traffic police, crime police, operations centre. It's hard to distinguish what's being talked about there, but it's to the chief of those operations. And, again, that's another one that's "for your information," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, tell me if I'm correct if I conclude, from looking at this, that if they're using the language "for your information," then what they're saying is this is just so you can know what is going on; and if they're not using that language, it means the organization it is sent to has specific tasks to fulfil with regard to that document. In other words, if it's not for your information, then it's for your action and for your responsibility to take action with regard to it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should be. But if we look at the substance of this document, you see that it is the secretariats of the interior that are in charge of taking these steps because they keep these records, as well as the border police stations that are expected to check any persons entering and leaving the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm really not interested in the substance right now. We may get into that with some other documents, but I now want to move on to another matter. I want to talk to you about the period of time in 1998 when you actually were in Kosovo. There was terrorist activity going on during the time you were there, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm wondering if you ever saw any volunteers among the ranks of the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. I worked in an office. I did sometimes go to the secretariats of the interior to familiarize myself with their methods and to meet my colleagues who were performing those jobs. I had no way of telling whether someone, a particular person, was a volunteer or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suppose that makes sense. Let me then ask you this: Did you ever see any personnel that were identified to you as being volunteers or as being paramilitaries that were among the ranks of the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such persons, and I don't think I would have been able to distinguish. I didn't know every single police officer. It wasn't possible. No one ever introduced another person to me as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it that if you -- if you didn't know whether you were seeing someone who was a volunteer or a paramilitary, then you wouldn't be able to tell us anything about what kind of uniforms were worn by the volunteers and the paramilitaries, would you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not something that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. It's 6D269. All right. We now got both versions on the screen. The first thing I want to call to your attention is there at the top, where it shows where this document was sent. You'll notice that one of the places it was sent was to the head of the MUP staff in Pristina, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was sent to all the organizational units, all the secretariats, all the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question I focused on was just: It was sent to the head of the MUP staff in Pristina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was also sent to the RDB, to the chief of the RDB, but it just says there "for information," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't say that it was sent to the head of the MUP staff just for information, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is dated 18 February 1999. You were still there at the time, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if you're familiar with this document. We can look at it if you want. In fact, we probably should look at the last page where the signature and name is. It appears to me that this came from General Djordjevic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It says head of the public security sector, Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go back now to paragraph 7; that's the paragraph that I'm basically interested in. We have it in English. Now we'll get it in Serbian. There it is. Now you should be able to see it. The translation I have says that this paragraph says this: "Through intensified intelligence and other measures and actions, carry out the necessary checks, compile lists, and establish complete control over volunteer and paramilitary units and their members." That's what that says, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is directed to the MUP staff, instructing them to do this, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The document says that it was forwarded to all the secretariats of the interior, not just the MUP staff. As to what this means, specifically I don't know and I don't wish to speculate. I could give you my opinion, though. Since in the territory of our country earlier on, there had been war operations. There were members of such volunteer units. I think they're being told here to establish some sort of control over them, so they knew what they were doing and so that they wouldn't come to Kosovo and Metohija to cause any problems or incidents there. That is my understanding of what it says. The police were gathering intelligence, and they knew of the fact that something like this existed. So the instruction here is for all the secretariats in all the areas, because there were people like this from all over Serbia, Belgrade, Novi Sad, and so on and so forth, to establish some sort of control to keep them from organizations themselves into units and to keep them from doing anything on their own and without any proper authorisation. So that's my understanding of what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you that your opinion and understanding of what that says is totally wrong, and we'll go into that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, we have to have a break at this stage for about 20 minutes or so. While we do that, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Vucurevic, we were talking about this document that's still on the screen, 6D269. At paragraph 7, it talks about compiling lists of these units and their members, so it's a two-phased operation, a list of the units and a list of their members. Did you ever see the lists that were compiled of the volunteer and paramilitary units and their members?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my line of work. I do not remember ever having seen such lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I have another document for you to look at then. It's 6D238. That first document we looked at, 6D269, was 18 February. This one's a little over a month later, 24 March of 1999; and, of course, you're still present there in Kosovo at this time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the addressees was the head of the MUP headquarters in Pristina, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't say "for your information," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It doesn't say "for your information."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the document comes from Vlajko Stojiljkovic, who was the minister, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, he says in this document directed to the head of the MUP staff in Pristina: "You shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members, and keep them under control in case that you might need to engage them," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that what it -- look at paragraph 5. According to the translation I have, it says: "You shall register all volunteer and paramilitary units and their members, and keep them under control in case that you might need to engage them," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what's written there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us a moment ago that you thought that initial order a month earlier was to keep them from coming into Kosovo, to get them under control and keep out of Kosovo; but this is talking about getting control of them and possibly engaging them, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what this is all about, and I don't want to engage in guess-work. I just presented my own view when you asked me in relation to the previous question, when you asked me what it meant, what I thought that it meant. As far as I can remember, as for the other document and this one, I don't remember having seen either one of them, or rather, I do not remember that anyone showed either one to me. In this paragraph, it doesn't say who it is that's supposed to do that, but I presented my view, my opinion. Once again, I underline that this is not my line of work. I'm not an expert in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you any more about that. I'm going to ask you about another document. It's P1989.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it will be on your screen. This is a document from the 4th of April of 1999. It says it's the minutes of a meeting with senior police officials in Kosovo and Metohija, and people there are Obrad Stevanovic, Major-General Sreten Lukic, the chiefs of all secretariats, PJP detachment commanders, SAJ commander, RDB, and JSO; so lots of people, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I know you were not there. I know you had already left Kosovo; but if you look -- I think it's probably on page 2, Colonel Dusan Gavranic makes a report. It is -- it's right there about halfway down page 2. And you'll notice Dusan Gavranic tells that group: "34 persons have been arrested so far, and there have been problems with volunteers in Zegra," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look now at P1990. We're back to 17 February of 1999 when you are still in Kosovo and Metohija. These are the minutes of a meeting of the MUP staff on that date. I don't know if you were present at that meeting or not, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at page -- probably on page 2, this might be difficult to find, but it -- General Lukic is speaking and he's talking about a plan of the RJB, the public security department. Can you find that? He says: "A plan of the RJB has been worked out to prevent and thwart entry of NATO troops in our territory." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "The Staff plans to carry out three mopping-up operations in the Podujevo, Dragobilje, and Drenica areas and has allocated around 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the operative," something, "group and around 900 police reservists." Now, that's something that Sreten Lukic said at this meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And he's clearly talking about a plan of the RJB, and he's clearly talking about a plan of the staff to carry out these mopping-up operations, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not my understanding of it. What is written here is that something will be carried out once it is ordered. Well, all these forces that are mentioned here, I understood that to be reporting to the minister as to the number of personnel of the police. Now, was it in that part of the territory, I really don't know. I cannot say with any accuracy because this was not my line of work. I heard about this more or less by way of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I hear what you're saying. Can you point me to the part of that paragraph which says that the staff plans to carry out these mopping-up operations when it is ordered? Where are the words "when it is ordered"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you allow me to read this in Serbian? The sentence precisely reads as follows: "The Staff planned to carry out, when this is ordered, three actions of mopping-up the terrain from terrorists ..." I don't need to read on any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So we have a bad translation I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So perhaps, Your Honour, this needs to be retranslated and resubmitted, because that does significantly change the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We will require that sentence to be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go over to, in the English, it's on page 5, and it's Minister Stojiljkovic who's speaking at this point, and it's very close to the end of what he has to say, right before a bunch of bullet points. I don't know if we'll find that in the Serbian or not; but according to the translation I have, he says this: "Within two or three days of an attack, we have to put our plans in motion and use the time to mop-up the territory from terrorists." And we've found it. It's just right above those bullet points. It's on the screen. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he speaks about "our plans," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know which plans the minister meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure, you know, when he talks about "our plans," it could have been any plans that had been put together by the MUP, but the plans he's talking about are something that he's going to put into action within two or three days after an attack to mop-up the territory from terrorists, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, finally, if you go down through those bullet points, you'll see some more language about volunteers where the minister says: "Approach and engage volunteers carefully, linking their engagement through the reserve police force when assessed as necessary," right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the minister meant by that, and I wouldn't like to engage in guess-work. Yet again, I can just give you my opinion. I know that the police does have a reserve force, so these are people who do their own work; and when necessary, they are engaged to do police work. All of these persons had completed their military service, and I think that it says here, "when we deem this necessary." So that is the only possibility that's referred to here, that somebody will be engaged when it is deemed necessary. I am not sure that all of these members, well, of the reserve police undergo training in order to be able to carry out police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to shift a little bit to something you may know a little more about, and it's in this same document. It's back right before Minister Stojiljkovic begins to speak. It's on page 3 in the English, and we're back to General Lukic again. And just to remind you, we're talking about 17 February of 1999, before the bombing started. General Lukic -- the paragraph begins with language, "the chiefs of SUP in Kosovo and Metohija and the PJP ..." And then down just a little bit, it's the paragraph right above where it says Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. General Luke says: "There have not been cases of Serbs leaving, but the number of requests from Siptars for travel documents and personal identity cards is on the rise." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it looks -- would you include from that that the Albanian residents in Kosovo were already starting to plan leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to intervene at this point, just that it's not Mr. Sreten Lukic who said this, but chiefs of SUPs, as it is written here in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine with me. I just misread it I think. He's right. It is chiefs of SUPs, which probably makes even more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that doesn't change my question. Would you agree with me that it looks like the Albanian residents of Kosovo were, as early as February, beginning to plan their departure?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. But I can say that, as far as I can remember, there was information to the effect that members of the KLA were exerting pressure on the Albanian population to move out of the territory of Kosovo in order to cause a humanitarian catastrophe; and, in this way, preconditions would be created for an aggression of NATO troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you now about another document. It's P1505, which we've seen many times recently, and you saw again today. This is that document of 16 June 1998 signed by Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister, his decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of the date on this document, 16 June 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it. I personally cannot recall the exact date; but if this says the 16th of June, then that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at the last page, please, and you see a stamp and a signature. Would you tell us what that stamp is and whose signature is there, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it's the minister's signature. The stamp is of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any reason, as you sit there now looking at that document, to doubt its genuineness and authenticity? It's a real document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since this is a photocopy, but it does have a signature and a stamp, there is no reason for me to doubt that this is a valid document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you see that this decision takes out of force, removes from force, three prior documents of 21 April, 15 May, and 11 June, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they're listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's fairly typical, if you're going to change a situation like members of a staff or something like that, you want to take out of force prior decisions and replace it with the new decision, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I want to know if you ever saw a decision after the 16th of June taking this 16 June decision out of force and rendering it not valid?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see such a decision, but I think I've already said that I'm not sure that I've seen these decisions before, those that are mentioned here and this decision of the 16th. I said that I only received a decision sending me personally to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. I really cannot remember whether anyone showed me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm really not even asking you if you ever saw it. It wouldn't have been directed to you in any event, would it? You wouldn't have been one of the recipients of it? It was to go to the head and the deputy head and the members of the staff and to the minister's office, right? So maybe it should have gone to you, as a member of the staff. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, the decision should always say who it was sent to; that is to say, all the recipients should be listed. And those persons who are recipients have to confirm with their own signature that they had received it, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've told us --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Write, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
