utterances.text: To write this in their own hand, to place their own handwritten signature there, including the date when it was submitted to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've told us that there are several things about this document that you think are not correct. There are six of those, as near as I can tell. The first one is you told us that David Gajic never served as deputy head of staff pursuant to this decision, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, is this not a matter for submission? Can we get to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe it is. I'll try to short-circuit, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there are six items in that document that you have told this Chamber are not correct and not true, were not implemented or were not true?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say now how many points I said were not true. We really have to move from one to another. When I was speaking, I wasn't speaking in terms of points, point 1, point 2, point 3. We'd really have to look at the decision, and then I could say what it is I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I thought, so we can do this rather quickly: The deputy head of staff, David Gajic; the assistant head for special operations, Milorad Lukovic; the paragraph that says "the expanded staff shall include chiefs of the secretariats"; the paragraph that says "other members of the ministry may be appointed to the staff on request of the head of staff"; and the next one is "the staff is tasked with planning, organizing, and managing," and it goes on and on; and the last one, "also the staff is tasked with planning, organizing, directing," and it goes on and on. In other words, each of those paragraphs, I think you told us on Friday, were not activated or were not true. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked at the beginning of my questioning of you about the importance of documents being correct and accurate. Can you explain to the Chamber how it is that this document, signed by the minister of the interior, could have six items in it that are just bogus, not true? How could that be? How could that happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot explain that. When we were talking about the personnel on the staff, I already said who I saw every day and who had an office there as a staff member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I mean, if this is the kind of documents that we find coming out of the MUP, can we rely on any MUP documents that we see in this case for being true and accurate? Do you think we can?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not a matter for the witness, Mr. Ackerman. A statement that wide is one for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally, let's go back to a document you saw earlier today, and that's P1990. You were asked about who the highest-ranking MUP officers were in Kosovo and Metohija, and you said that Stevanovic and Djordjevic at various times were the highest-ranking officers. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this is a meeting from 17 February of 1999, and present are both of those people, Vlastimir Djordjevic and Obrad Stevanovic, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it looks like the person in control of the meeting is General Sreten Lukic. He opened the meeting; he did virtually all of the speaking. Finally, Minister Stojiljkovic speaks starting on page 3 of the English, but General Lukic seems to be basically leading the meeting and in charge, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, all I can give you is my opinion. It says here that the -- this is a record of a meeting that was held at the staff. General Sreten Lukic was the host, and he probably opened this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And General Djordjevic only spoke right at the very end, where he said five officers were promoted. That was his only contribution, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Vucurevic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that, from 1991 until 1992, you were employed with the state security sector of the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's just that it wasn't called sector at the time. It was State Security Service. I said "sector" just to make myself clear because that's what it's called now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What was the general nature of your work in state security?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as an operative there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you change from state security to public security?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there were certain changes in terms of personnel that were occurring of the secretariat of the interior in Novi Sad. The head of the secretariat was replaced. We knew each other, so he asked to see me and he asked me whether I would agree to work as a head of a department. I accepted that since that in my case was a promotion. So it was for that reason that I went back to work with the secretariat of the interior in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. After 1992, did you maintain any contact or did you do any work for the state security side of the house?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I no longer worked for the State Security Service because I had my own job. I did have a number of contacts because I knew a number of people who I worked with. Some of those were acquaintances and some or friends. Then of course was the department that I was working for. There were contacts with the State Security Service in terms of us forwarding to them lists of foreigners who were entitled to temporary or permanent residence in Novi Sad territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us, at page 23041, line 22, that your primary line of work was to maintain contacts with international humanitarian organizations, and I think that referred to 1998 and 1999 before the war started in Kosovo; is that correct? Is that the time-period you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who instructed you on how you were to interact with those international organizations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I left for Pristina, I had spent two days consulting with the border police administration. This was an administration that I, too, belonged to. They explained in brief what my remit would be at the MUP staff in Pristina. It was then that I learned that I would be receiving operations reports from the border police station, and that there were humanitarian non-governmental organizations that were active in Kosovo and Metohija; and I was also told that I would be in touch with them, that I would be familiarizing myself with their methods and with their work, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the persons who instructed you about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had spoken to the person who was then the head of the department for foreigners in the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember whether I spoke to Mr. Dujkovic, too, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the person besides Mr. Dujkovic that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milorad Urdarevic, I think, but I'm not certain because different people came and went, different heads; and I can't quite put my finger on it, but I think he was the person at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were first sent to Kosovo pursuant to a decision of General Djordjevic on the 9th of March, 1998, and we've seen Exhibit 6D1048.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's a handwritten note on it: "Received 19th March, 1998," and I believe you told us that's your signature. Do you remember what you were told at the time you received this document? I mean, did anyone explain to you why you were being sent there and what they expected you to do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was served this document by the then-chief of the Novi Sad SUP, Mr. Kresoja. There was a replacement in the leadership of the Novi Sad SUP that year, and Mr. Kresoja was now there to replace Mr. Zavisic. I was on annual leave on Mount Zlatibor with my children. Mr. Dujkovic phoned me and said that I was now appointed to the MUP staff of the Republic of Serbia in Pristina. It was on my return from annual leave that this decision was served.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone explain to you what your duties were supposed to be as part of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina; and if so, who was that and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me specifically what my duties were supposed to be, nor was I shown an actual decision setting up this staff or, for that matter, any other document listing my rights and duties. We talked and I was told that, as I said, I would be receiving reports and information; and whenever the chief of the staff required, I would be reporting to him as far as my line of work was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In that answer, you just made when you say "we talked," are you referring to the people from the border administration?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you just said in your answer: "We talked and I was told that ... I would be receiving reports and information ..." When you say "we talked," are you referring to Dujkovic and Urdarevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in addition to Dujkovic, I think I spoke to him; and Urdarevic, I am sure about him, though. I think I also spoke to the head of the border police administration. I think that was Mr. Bogdanovic. I had spoken to two chiefs who briefly told me what I have just conveyed to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you actually arrived in Kosovo, did anybody from the MUP staff in Pristina explain to you what your job was to include? Anybody in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that anybody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the MUP staff when you first arrived in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first arrived in 1998, the chief of the MUP staff was Mr. Aco Vesovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after you arrived in Kosovo and worked for the staff, who did you report to about your contacts with international humanitarian organizations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I've stated this already; but as far as I know, the greatest number of contacts were with the International Red Cross and the High Commissioner for Refugees, and this was something that was done by Mr. Vesovic. I was in touch with other NGOs, for example, Medecins Sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe it was a translation problem. My question was: Who did you report to about your contacts with international humanitarian organizations? Were you reporting to the border police administration or to Mr. Vesovic or both?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not report to the administration about those contacts. Initial contacts were just for me to get to know these organizations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vesovic. We had occasional meetings, I would say. I had been in touch with this or that organization, I got to know their leaders, I got to know about their activities, and that was the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And were those oral reports or written reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oral.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often? Once a day? Once a week?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember. Probably once a week, sometimes more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have we seen any documents compiled by this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you ever write reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in relation to my job. I did write reports, as I said. Sometimes, we would get daily overviews of what was going on, after the Kosovo Verification Mission had been set up, and I was in charge of some technical business there for Mr. Mijatovic. As far as I remember, the reports were signed either by Mr. Mijatovic or by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What you just described, were those the daily reports on security matters that went to the minister and Djordjevic and Rade Markovic and others in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think there was a dispatch determining precisely that the ministry should be informed about this; who were the Kosovo verification people in touch with, I mean who from the Ministry of the Interior; what were the questions and what were the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Back to your contacts with international humanitarian organizations, you told us about your oral reports to Vesovic. Did you have any interaction or contact or sharing of that information with the DB, with state security?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no interaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to those interactions with the international humanitarian organizations, you told us, at page 23042, that you sometimes warned them that in certain areas you couldn't guarantee their safety. With regard to those kind of warnings, did you personally convey those warnings?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember specifically but I do think so. I do think that I did. They would phone me to announce their ambition to visit certain areas, and then I would tell them that a specific area was not under the control of the MUP. Back in 1998, we were having a very difficult year in Kosovo and Metohija because most of the roads, so to speak, were under the control of the terrorists, members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you -- when you did pass along those kind of warnings, did you make any kind of written record of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no official notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any unofficial notes? Did you keep any kind of diary yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no notebook, but I recorded whatever it was that I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So would you still have records of those kind of warnings that you had conveyed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such records. These records were destroyed when the SUP building in Pristina was targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me see here. I'd like to have you take a look at Exhibit 6D262. This is a dispatch from the ministry dated the 18th of June, 1998, from the minister. Do you recall having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it does talk about some of the international humanitarian organizations, including the Red Cross and the UNHCR. Do you know to whom it was further circulated to, because we see it going to the ministry staff in Pristina, but did you independently make any further circulation of it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not circulate this document to anyone. As far as I can tell, all the organizational units of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can see, on the first page, there's some handwritten notations. You see those?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm able to read it properly. It says police department; traffic police, OSP; and then OKP, crime police department; and then this is quite illegible, but I think what it says is OPP, might be border police department; followed by PS, police stations; SSP, meaning traffic police stations; and, finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's okay. I want to ask you to look at the last page as well of the B/C/S. It looks like two handwritten lines in the first paragraph on that page and another handwritten line at the bottom of that second one. Do you know who wrote those in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't suppose you can tell us whether those handwritten entries were on the document received at the MUP staff when it got there or if they were put on later. You're not able to tell us about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the space between these lines, I think there's a line missing or it simply can't be found in the document. Probably something was left out, but I really don't know who wrote this and for what reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the very last entry on that page, in the bottom left, is typed the number "2" and then two words, which looks mike "kom" and then "cirk." Do you know what "2 kom cirk" means?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that in your job with the staff you received reports from border police stations, and you informed the staff leader or the manager of any security-related events. Would you -- during your last few days at the MUP staff, after the bombing started and before you were injured, did you receive any reports from the border police station about the number of people leaving Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether I received a separate report or whether this was part of the normal reporting done by the secretariat of the interior. However, as far as I remember, there was a bulletin that we produced. I produced some of those myself, and we spoke about the situation that prevailed at the border crossings, and something that had been observed was Albanians, people of Albanian ethnicity, leaving the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I think there was a specific report in relation to each day in terms of how many people left on each given day and what the breakdown was for these people leaving. As far as I remember, for the most part, the people leaving were ladies and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've seen another document from the end of April, after you were already gone, in which there is an indication of the number of Siptars who left. Now, I think you told us earlier today in your testimony that at the border station it wouldn't be normal process to ask for identity documents, and it wasn't necessarily a requirement to have ethnic information on those documents. How was that information being gathered and reported to the MUP staff about the ethnicity of those people leaving?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever someone tries to leave the country, their travel documents are checked, the name and surname. Based on a person's name, you can conclude whether this person is, in fact, an ethnic Serb or a member of the Albanian ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in that document that I was referring to, it's in P1693, it indicates that by the 30th of April, some 718.000 Siptars had left Kosovo. Are you telling us that all of those people had travel documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about the time that I spent in Pristina and about them leaving with travel documents on them. I really know nothing about how they were leaving at a later stage, and I don't wish to speculate whether they had any travel documents or not, whether they were checked or were, in fact, not checked. By this time, I had already sustained an injury and I was off sick. I didn't even follow the press on a regular basis at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, during the first week of the war, we have evidence in this case that tens if not hundreds of thousands of Kosovar Albanians left Kosovo in that first week of the war. Is it your position that they all had travel documents that had to be shown and checked before they were allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that in relation to the previous period. After the air-strikes had begun, and I can't remember the exact day, I think I was told at one point about something at the border crossing of Vrbnica and the fact that there were people there who were leaving the country with no travel documents. I can't be entirely certain, but I think there was a report like that that reached the MUP staff, yet I can't remember whether I, in fact, told Mr. Lukic about this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the report stated that those people had left and that everything had been resolved by an agreement between that particular border crossing and the border police administration that was within the MUP. This was a single day before my injury, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is your only information about that written information in a report from the border police? Is that your only information about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, indeed, if there were such a report, it would come to you given the nature of your job, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not receiving interpretation right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That kind of report from the border police about Siptar civilians leaving would have come to you because of the nature of your job, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border police station would have sent something like this along to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And wouldn't you automatically have conveyed that information to General Lukic? You just said you can't remember whether you did or not. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is I can't remember, but I can't remember specifically whether this was a Friday or a Saturday. As far as I remember, the Chief of Staff and some other members of the staff had moved on to a different location outside the Pristina SUP building. And if I remember correctly, the only people remaining back at the building were Mr. Adamovic, Mr. Slovic, and I. It was perhaps for that reason that I didn't inform Mr. Lukic. Perhaps, I simply didn't know his whereabouts at the time. But as far as I remember, if there was a document that said that something had been resolved, that meant that it had been resolved and would have implied no urgency in terms of me needing to get in touch with General Lukic immediately and report this to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a member of the MUP staff after General Lukic had arrived in July of 1998, how frequently would have contact with him? Daily? Once or twice a week? How often?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, when Mr. Lukic came, we had meetings more frequently than in Mr. Vesovic's time. Now, was it twice a week or perhaps at first it was every day, because there was the need for us to get to know Mr. Lukic. Later on, I saw him only when it was necessary; that is to say, that I attended certain meetings between Mr. Lukic and members of the Kosovo Verification Mission and members of the UNHCR and the International Committee of the Red Cross. I think I actually took the minutes of those meetings. Of course, when they wanted to have contact with Mr. Lukic, I mean international humanitarian organizations, they would first talk to me, asking me when he had the time to see them, and then I would schedule their meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic asked you about your personal role in daily reporting. You explained that you received reports about state security. Those reports were reviewed, and you said: "We also wrote a report that we sent to the ministry." And with regard to this information, you said: "Yes. Analytical processing did take place, and only the most important events would be included in these reports." Who in the MUP staff did that analysis that you described in your answer?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a correction here. What I heard mentioned here was that we received reports from the state security sector. I never received or saw any such reports, and the State Security Service did not submit any kind of reports to us. As for your question, this work was carried out by Mr. Slovic. He was the analyst and he compiled these reports. From time to time, I would stand in for him when he would go away for a weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. In further describing your work at the staff, you were asked about what legal regulations you applied in the course of your work. You said you did, indeed, use many laws; first of all, the Law on the Personal Identity Card, then the Law on Domicile and Residence, and the Law on Travel Documents. What exactly was the work that you were doing on the staff that involved using these laws?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then this was not properly translated either. As far as I can remember, Mr. Lukic asked me what regulations I applied in the course of my work as head of the department, or rather, what regulations are applied in the line of work that I belonged to. I did not state that I applied all these regulations while on the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What did you do on the staff besides these contacts with international humanitarian organizations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any other duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I understand the decision appointing you to work on the MUP staff, did you not get additional pay for that assignment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. All who were sent there received, on account of lives separate from their families and I don't know for what other reasons, a salary that was 50 per cent higher than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about your appointment then, and let's look again at Exhibit P -- or 6D1048. This is the decision by General Djordjevic appointing you. It makes reference to the fact that you're being dispatched to carry out the duties and tasks of the assistant head of staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for it to come up on the screen so we can all follow along.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It makes reference to that staff. It says: "Formed by a decision of the deputy minister, head of public security department ST 01, strictly confidential number 2793/93 of 15 April 1994." Did you ever see that decision that's referenced there, the one from 15 April 1994? Do you know what it says?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this decision by General Djordjevic, in addition to that reference, in the very first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to Article 72 of the Law on Internal Affairs and Article 2 on the Law on Employment," the decision was made to send you there. I ask you to keep that in mind, and I want to refer you now to Exhibit P1251. I'll give you a hard copy of this because I'm actually going to ask you to speak to both 1251 and 1252 in sequence, so I'll hand you both. You see, in P1251, there's a printed number in the bottom right of that page. This is a decision on the formation of the staff of the ministry in Pristina. And the top of the page, it says: "Pursuant to Article 10 of the Book of Rules on the," it says, "International Organization of the Ministry of the Interior." I assume that's a typo, and it should be the "Internal Organization of the Ministry of the Interior"; is that right? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here: "Rules on the Internal Organization of the Ministry of the Interior ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the Book of Rules of the Internal Organization are? Are you familiar with those?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we say that that is a book of rules on systemization. I've never actually seen the entire Book of Rules. I've just seen excerpts from it. But these rules clearly refer to all the organizational units of the ministry and all the jobs therein. Every organizational unit has its own number and every job has its own number. While I worked there, I just received the rules on the organization of my own department. I did not have insight into the entirety of these rules; that is to say, that every head would receive only that which pertained to his own unit, that is to say, what the number was of that particular organizational unit and how many jobs were in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see a copy of this decision prior to coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Let me just have a look. I saw some decision, but I don't know if it was this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could look at the very bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S and it's item number 2(e) in the English on the first page, among the task of the staff, it includes: "Training organized units to perform successfully special security assignments ..." It goes on to talk about "special units of the police, special anti-terrorist units, and mechanised brigades of the police for proceeding according to Kolubara-1." That looks like the name of a plan. Do you know what Kolubara-1 was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to page 2 of the English and the B/C/S, number 4 indicates that: "The composition of the staff will be laid down in a separate decision," which we'll see in a minute in P1252. Item number 5 says: "The staff leader is responsible to the chief of the public security department for his own work and the work of the staff ..." To your knowledge, to whom did General Lukic report during his tenure as Chief of Staff or head of the staff in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it says here that he is responsible to the head of the sector, then he was responsible to the head of the sector and the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you'll go down to number 8, it says: "This decision supersedes the decision on the formation of the staff of the Ministry of the Interior for the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija ..." It makes reference to that confidential number of 15 April 1994 that we saw in Exhibit 6D1048 that appointed you to the staff, right? You may want to refer back to 6D1048, which was the document that appointed you to the staff of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see where this number is. If you're referring to 2793/93 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll look --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's the same document it's referring to, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this seems to show that the staff was established in 1994 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. That decision establishing a staff in April of 1994 is the one under which you were appointed to the staff in March of 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand what the question is. I mean, I can say if what you mean is what number this is. In the decision, it says it is the staff that is organized in 1994; whereas, here it says that this decision was no longer in force. So this is contradictory to one another, unless I have a careful look at the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the contradiction's resolved by the next document, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't know that analysing it with the witness is really all that helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he is a lawyer and he was on the MUP staff, and he's my best chance, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Be patient with me, sir, we need to go through about two more documents to get to the end of this. Now, if you will look at 1252, that's another document from General Djordjevic, and this is naming the leaders and members of the staff of Ministry of the Interior for the autonomous province of Kosovo. Number 1 is General Lukic. Number 8 is yourself. I think in the English translation your name is not spelled correctly, but I believe it's clearly you. You see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes; although, it's not a very legible copy, but I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I apologise for that. That seems to be the best copy we have. And on the back page or the second page, we see a date that's sort of illegible. We have the date of 11, something, 1998. I think, from other evidence, you'll probably find that it's probably the 11th of June, 1998. Now I need to take you to P1505, which is one that you've seen a couple of times already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Taking, though, these two together, 1251 and 1252, Mr. Vucurevic, do you see that they in combination appear to replace the 1994 document under which you were originally appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what it says in the last paragraph, that by the adoption of this decision, 1251, that is, the other decision from 1994 shall no longer be in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So 1251 creates a different staff and 1252 appoints personnel to that staff who may largely have been there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like you to take a look at P1505, and you may have it. I have a hard copy if you want, so you can look at these all at the same time. This is a decision by the minister.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. They took those papers away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, we'll give you 1251 and 1252 to keep for a while. This is a decision by the minister dated the 16th of June, 1998. And the first thing I'd like you to look at is on the last page, page 3 of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English, item number 6. It says: "With this decision coming into force, the following shall come out of force ..." There's a reference to a decision to establish an operational staff of 21 April 1998. I don't know what that is. I don't think we've seen that one here yet. But then there's a reference to the decision to establish a staff of the ministry and dated the 15th of May, 1998. It makes reference to number 1206/98. I think if you look at that document, even though there are some parts that are difficult to read, you'll agree with me that that must be a reference to P1251? Would you agree, based on the name of the decision and the date and the number, that that's probably what it refers to there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two decisions are referred to here, the decision on the establishment of 1998 and then yet another decision from May 1998, and the third decision is on the appointment of the actual composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And, right now, I'm trying to go step by step. Would you agree with me the one from May of 1998 is Exhibit P1251 entitled: "Decision to establish a staff of the Ministry of the Interior for the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is clear here, the 15th of May, 1998. Yes, that's the decision. That is Exhibit P0251.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the last one referred to here in item 6 is the decision on the appointment of the staff group; that is, the head and members of the staff of the ministry, 11 June 1998. Would you take a look at 1252, P1252, and would you agree with me that that's what it must be referring to here in P1505?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that's it because you can see here the 11th, you cannot see the month, and you can see 1998. And if you look at the very name where it says appointing the actual composition, that corresponds to what this decision says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this portion of this decision to take out of force those two prior decisions of General Djordjevic does not make any reference to that April 1994 decision that was referenced in your appointment; do you agree with me there? There's no reference to that confidential number 2793/93 of 15 April 1994?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So when 1251 and 1252 were taken out of force, then, in effect, the April 1994 decision is reinstated and now is in force, and that was the one under which you were appointed; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what these decisions said. It's a bit strange that a decision from 1994 would be in force and other things that were adopted after that would not be in force. I don't know whether this is still in force or whether it is being superseded by something else. It is illogical that a document that was passed earlier on is later on changed with another document or amended by another document, and then a third document is passed saying that the first one is no longer valid. I'm don't know if I'm being clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but Perhaps this is a good time for our lunch break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly am not clear how it is revived, if that is what you are suggesting, Mr. Hannis. Bearing in mind also that in P1505, this witness is named as one of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, and we'll address that a little further after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We need another break at this stage, Mr. Vucurevic, this will be for half an hour. Would you again leave the court with the usher, and we shall resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I want to continue with Exhibit P1505, that 16 June 1998 decision. Would you take a close look at the title of that decision on the first page. My English translation says: "Decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Decision on the establishment of a staff of the ministry for the suppression of terrorism."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's all in capital letters, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of it is in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you'll look at P1251, which I think you still have there, that was the 15th of May, 1998 decision by General Djordjevic. You'll see that one I think says: "Decision on the formation of a staff of the ministry in Pristina"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is stated in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And one more, if you will, is the decision that appointed you in March 1998. Exhibit 6D01048 said you were dispatched to carry out the duties and tasks of assistant head of staff of the Ministry of the Interior in Pristina, formed by a decision of the deputy minister, et cetera. So those two earlier documents from March 1998, your appointment document, and the decision in 1251 simply refer to a staff of the ministry in Pristina; whereas, 1505 is referring to a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism. Were there two separate staffs, one particularly devoted to the suppression of terrorism and another one that was just a general, more administrative kind of staff in Kosovo? Isn't that one way we can try and understand how all these documents work together?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was just one staff of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. I do not know of the existence of any other staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And even though your name in P1505 as a member of this ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism, I think your testimony before was that you don't recall ever having seen this document or received a copy of it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that when you were there, in 1998, you said David Gajic was not a member of the staff. Do you know who David Gajic was? Did you ever meet him personally?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used to see him in the Pristina SUP lunchroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Milorad Lukovic, also known as Legija, in Kosovo in either 1998 or 1999 before you left?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw him once, too, in that same hall, and I asked myself who he was -- rather, I asked the question, and then I can't remember who exactly it was who answered the question and said that was Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about Colonel Zivko Trajkovic, did you ever meet him or know who he was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I met Zivko Trajkovic at one of the meetings at the staff, and I can't remember whether there was any other time that I met him, but I knew who he was. I knew based on what people had told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us that Miroslav Mijatovic was the deputy head, but I understand he didn't arrive until sometime in mid-July 1998. Who was the deputy head of staff when you first arrived in Kosovo and before Mr. Mijatovic came?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first arrived in April 1998, and as far as I know, the deputy head of staff was Mr. Radislav Djinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember right now whether it was the head of staff who told me, Mr. Vesovic, or the other members of the staff that I found there. We were then introduced to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In answer to a question about this document where there's a reference to the expanded staff, including chiefs of secretariats and centres and branches of the RDB, you said, at page 23057: "I don't know what this term 'expanded staff' means." Sir, you're a lawyer. You must have some idea of what "expanded staff" means in this context, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's what I said. I think the question was were they members of the staff, and my answer was I did not see them at the staff regularly, only every now and then when the minister of the interior was there or one of the aforementioned generals when the meetings were held at the staff itself. My assumption is this: If a body had been set up, then every now and then it would have had to meet in its complete set-up, so that everybody knew what they had to do; and then there would be another meeting to see what the result of those actions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Goran Radosavljevic having an office in the same area where you other members of the staff were located. What was your understanding of his job on the MUP staff in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what his specific job was; but based on what I knew about his qualifications, and I think he had told me this, himself, that he was into training police units, my conclusion at the time was that he was there on behalf of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The nature of your job was such that you really didn't have much involvement with that part of the MUP that dealt with the PJP and the SAJ, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Throughout my career, I never worked in a police department or administration. I never wore a uniform. I was a civilian working for the Ministry of the Interior. I knew that there were such units around, but I never learned exactly what the scope of their activity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about whether the MUP staff had the ability to change any order that arrived from the Ministry of the Interior, and you explained, no, it did not, because it didn't have the power to change orders not issued by them. That leads to my question of: In fact, did not the MUP staff issue certain orders or instructions or directions to either the SUP or PJP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer about my own line of work based on what I remember. The head of staff or I myself never directly issued an order. There may be one exception, and I can't remember specifically, but I think it was about the Kosovo Verification Mission or about the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. I had looked at quite many documents, and I can't be certain now, but I think there was this one situation where we sent a letter to all the secretariats throughout the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we take a look now at Exhibit 6D768. I can hand you a hard copy of this one, and I think you can return those others now. I'm done with 1505 and 1251 and 1252, I think. This is a document dated the 7th of August, 1998, from General Lukic to the SUP in Pristina, Pec, Prizren, Djakovica, et cetera, and to the commander of the PJP joint detachment. Have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw it during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We know from other witnesses and documents that there was some joint VJ and MUP actions, anti-terrorist actions, in late July and early August 1998. In paragraph 2 here, you see there's a reference to: "After actions or operations had been carried out, it was noticed that certain police officers in manoeuvre and territorial detachments and members of the reserve force, including officers in those units, behaved highly unprofessionally." It mentions stealing from houses, stealing vehicles, torching houses, et cetera. Were you aware that there were complaints or concerns about that problem in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard that there were problems, but I can't be certain now. I think this even was mentioned in the daily reports that were sent to the Ministry of the Interior. I'm not certain if there was perhaps a meeting where someone from one of the humanitarian organizations came up with this, what we see stated here, but I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you'll go on down to the fourth paragraph, it's two below the one that I just read from. It says: "There are many diplomatic and consular representatives in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, many representatives of the International Red Cross and other international organizations, as well as journalists who move around, shoot footage, and take photographs." In your job as contact with the international humanitarian organizations, do you not recall that some of them were bringing to your attention complaints about that kind of conduct by the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I think this was something that was done by the International Red Cross Committee. I think they mentioned several times their information on things that had been done by police officers on the ground; unprofessional things, illegitimate things, and illegal things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you include in any of the reports that you assisted in that kind of information, those complaints from the internationals about police misconduct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended meetings and I think that everything that is stated here was included in the report. However, representatives of the ICRC or any other organization were, as far as I remember, always required to state exactly the time and place that something happened, so that all the facts and circumstances might be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you'll go on, in light of these mentioned problems, General Lukic says: "In order to fight and prevent such occurrences, it's necessary to do the following," and he lists three things. Number 1: "Ensure full control over employees of the ministry." Number 2: "Vigorously institute criminal and misdemeanour disciplinary proceedings." Number 3: "Record all such instances and events and immediately inform the staff of the ministry in Pristina." The last paragraph says: "Chiefs in the secretariat and commanders of the PJP joint detachment shall be personally responsible for the implementation of the above measures and for preventing such occurrences." Now, this document is not entitled, "Order," but that reads to me like that's an order, that's a direction to the SUPs and the PJP, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not entitled, "Order," but again this document, too, was probably produced based on contacts with representatives of international organizations. If you ask me, it has the nature of instructions. This is something, instructions, that should be followed, because what we see stated at the end of this document, that the heads of secretariats were responsible, well that's nothing new. They are normally responsible for ensuring that all their members work in a way that is legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that it is not entitled: "Order," but my question is: In real life, how did that work? Were the SUP chiefs and the PJP commander free to ignore this without any consequences?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this worked in practical terms and whether they were, in fact, free to ignore anything. But I know that I previously stated that I remember criminal complaints being brought against members of the Ministry of the Interior who were found to have committed crimes, and I think this was actually included in the reports that were dispatched to the ministry. Each member of the secretariat is responsible for taking disciplinary action as soon as they learn that something has been done. If it's a crime, then people from the crime police join in, and members of the ministry are treated exactly the same way and on the same terms as any other citizen who commits a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, based on your answer, this document, would you not agree with me that General Lukic appears to have the authority to issue such a direction and that those who received it, the SUP chiefs and the commander of the PJP, abided by it because you tell me they took actions against those who misbehaved?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is, above all, a warning, since all the international organizations, first and foremost, would address the head of staff and not the chiefs of the secretariats. Certain irregularities had been observed in the conduct of the police, and this was a reminder that measures ought to be taken and that everyone ought to be taking measures within their own field of competence. As far as I know, representatives of international organizations only presented their remarks to the staff of the ministry, I mean those remarks that actually had to do with the conduct of members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as a lawyer, are you saying this document has no legal effect, or is this an area outside your expertise?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean that this has no legal effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, does this carry more weight than if I'd written a letter to the SUP and the PJP and said, "Don't do that again," and make sure that everybody follows the rules? Doesn't General Lukic have higher standing, or is he just writing this document to hear his own words? If this is not an order, what is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is and I don't wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I gave you is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis's first question might have been helpful if he had just adhered to it. Does it have any more force than if Mr. Hannis had written to the SUP chiefs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think any random citizen could send a letter like this to people working for the Ministry of the Interior. There could have been an individual letter by an individual citizen about particular violations of his rights by a member of the Ministry of the Interior in the line of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, we've had evidence in this case of citizens writing to the ministry to tell them about general problems, international organizations observing the situation and then communicating with members of the government and government departments. Now, does the letter from Mr. Lukic have any greater force than a letter from some international humanitarian organization saying, "Please obey the rules"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this is a document that was, after all, signed and dispatched by an officer of the Ministry of the Interior who had knowledge, I suppose, to the effect that there had been the cases of unprofessional conduct. He wanted to, again, draw everyone's attention to the fact that they were under an obligation to obey the law and implement the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but why should this have any more force because it comes from Mr. Lukic, or are you, in fact, saying it doesn't have any force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure you understand me correctly. Given the fact that international humanitarian organizations were in touch with the ministry staff, and as I said we were receiving reports from all the different secretariats, this is a summary of all of that, and that was why it was probably dispatched to all the secretariats of the interior as a general description of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vucurevic, I want to ask you now about 6D798. I'll hand you a hard copy of this one. I think you saw it before. It's the minutes of a meeting held on 22 July at the Pristina MUP conference hall. Do you recall having seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're listed as one of the persons in attendance. Do you remember being at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I looked at the document, I remembered that I had attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see on the agenda the three different items. Would you read out number 3 for us, because I think there's been an issue about the translation of one term in there. Could you read out loud what that says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3 reads: "Defining tasks about the implementation of the global plan and the tasks to come."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, from other evidence, we've heard that General Lukic and some others had been at a meeting shortly before this with President Milosevic and General Pavkovic and other representatives of the army and the MUP. What was said at this meeting about that plan that you just read out in item number 3? What do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically all the things that were said at the meeting, but basically I heard that there was some sort of a plan and I think they talked about the different stages of that plan. I don't know the exact number of these stages, maybe between 3 and 5, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you give us any more detail about the nature of that plan, a plan to do what?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already stated, and I believe I did state that once at least, the situation that prevailed in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija at the time was very difficult. As far as I remember, the only road that was clear was the one leading from Pristina to Urosevac. The one from Prizren to Pec could not be taken. There were daily attacks along that road. I even think that some of those roads were closed. That was my understanding of the reason for this plan. It was meant to clear the road so that the citizens might again be able to travel unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who took the minutes of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all the minutes were taken by Mr. Slovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You'll notice that this document ends after the remarks by the Gradimir Zekavica from the Prizren SUP, and he's apparently only the third SUP commander or chief to speak. Do you know what happened to the rest of the minutes for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll notice the second page just stops after one paragraph and is completely blank after that. Do you know why this document is in that condition?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if the other two items on the agenda are assessment of the security situation in the territory covered by the secretariat and an assessment of the situation in the units, from what I've seen in other minutes of these kind of meetings, would it not be typical for pretty much all those SUP chiefs and all those PJP commanders to make at least a few brief remarks? That's usual what happened at these meetings, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. If you ask me, each of them should have reported about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't remember any comment by General Lukic or Djordjevic or Stevanovic about their opinion of this plan at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any concerns they had about the MUP's role in that plan?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vucurevic, during your time there with MUP staff, did you hear anything about the term "the armed non-Siptar population"? Did you ever hear that term used?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember a term like that being used. There is something that I think was called "reserve police."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is my next question. What did you know about the reserve police and the reserve police stations in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know much about that. I said that I heard the term being used, "reserve police squad." I can't remember whether this was at a meeting, but I think that their role was to perform police business in those areas where there weren't a sufficient number of police around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any idea of the numbers of reserve police stations that were being organized in 1998 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I truly didn't know that. I didn't know their strength. I simply heard the term used; that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any information about who was providing weapons to those reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't remember, but if -- I really don't know who was providing weapons to them. I can't say. I wasn't involved in that; therefore, I can hardly be expected to speculate and possibly provide answers that might prove erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you now Exhibit P1224. I think you saw this document earlier. This is dated the 18th of October, 1998, and it's described as a summary of the numbers of policemen in Kosovo and Metohija on 16 October. Do you recall having seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who actually compiled the information in the attached tables and who put together the text in this summary?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who it was that did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know when that was done? We see the dates on there, but ...

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can just see that this is a review of the situation on the 16th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you will look at the organization chart which I think you talked about before, you commented that there was no reference to the MUP staff. But is it correct that this document was supposed to reflect all policemen in Kosovo at that time? That's what it purports to be, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document does include all policemen, as far as I can see. All the SUPs are listed here, all the police stations, and I'm looking at the abbreviations here as well. Even the special anti-terrorist unit is referred to there and the station of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So these are employees of the ministry who we call policemen who wear uniforms and carry weapons. That is what I am particularly highlighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What can you tell me with regard to the reference to the SAJ under the SUP in Pristina on this organization chart? There's a word "alvalija." What does that mean? Is that a location?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here it says, "SAJ alvalija." As far as I know, there were three anti-terrorist organizations SAJ in Belgrade, Novi Sad, and Pristina. What is written here, "ajvalija," I think that's a part of town where their headquarters is or the premises where they were put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this number doesn't purport to reflect the number of reserve policemen or the reserve police stations that had been formed by this date, correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that here. I can -- I really cannot say anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I don't know whether they were stated separately or whether they were in the regular police stations. I am really not aware of their structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think mentioning RPO as stations could cause some confusion, because I think the other day we clarified that those are not stations but squads, RPO. They didn't have any stationary objects in which they were placed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's correct Mr. Hannis, on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll accept that, Your Honour. I was just reading from a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you then, sir, about the purpose of that document. Based on the timing and the numbers reflected therein, it seems to me that that may have been prepared in relation to the discussions with internationals that eventually led to the October agreements regarding Kosovo. Is that correct or do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is correct. I mean, I cannot remember the exact date when the number of members of the Ministry of the Interior was supposed to be reduced in the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. I assume that that is why this document was compiled, in order to have a review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your time in Kosovo in 1998 and until the beginning April 1999, did you ever hear the term "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija"?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I heard it once at one of the meetings; although, I cannot remember exactly who it was that had used the term. But I do not remember that I particularly memorised that term or that I paid any attention to it. It wasn't clear to me what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'll have you take a quick look at Exhibit P2086. This is a meeting on I think it's the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think I gave you the wrong number. I need 2805. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a meeting on the 5th of November, 1998. You're listed as being in attendance. I'll hand you a hard copy. And in addition to the minister, President Milutinovic, several citizens, General Pavkovic, and some 13 representatives of the army, among other regular attendees, were present at this meeting. Do you recall that meeting where President Milutinovic came and spoke?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that I was present at that meeting. As far as I can remember, that was the only time that President Milutinovic was in Pristina. I think that he talked about resolving the problems of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in his remarks, in page 3 of the English - I'm not sure where it is exactly in your copy - he does make reference to the Joint Command. Do you think that's where you might have heard the term was in this meeting where President Milutinovic made reference to it? He said: "Everything remains the same for the Yugoslav Army; and police, Joint Command, VJ units are not withdrawing and police forces are reduced only by the part that has already been withdrawn." Does that refresh your memory about when you might have heard the term?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what it was that you underlined and that is in brackets here, I think that that's the first time when I heard that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you not aware that General Lukic attended dozens of meetings of the Joint Command just between the 22nd of July and the end of October, 1998, while you were there as a member of the MUP staff? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what meetings General Lukic went to. He was my superior officer; I wasn't his. So I really don't know who he went to meet and what he discussed at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nor do you know what kind of plans may have been discussed at those meetings, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't take part in such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I know you left around the 1st of April; but in your preparations to testify, did anyone show you a decree that was signed by President Milutinovic concerning identity cards that was signed, I think, on the 31st of March, 1999, changing the law on identity cards? Did you see that in preparing to testify?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 1D144, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can hand you a copy of this, sir. The cover page is a letter from the Deputy Prime Minister, Professor Markovic, and the text of the decree is on, I think, the second page. I'm particularly interested in Article 3 that says: "A person who loses a personal identity card or is not in possession of said for some other reason is obliged to report it within 24 hours to the competent organizational unit of the Ministry of the Interior in the place where the personal identification card was lost." My first question: The competent organizational unit in this context would be, what, the SUP in that location?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat of the interior in terms of the residence of the person to whom a personal identity card had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, here, it would be the SUP in the area where the card was lost, rather than where it was issued, right? That's where they're supposed to report the loss or other circumstances under which they came to be without it, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't read this very precisely. It says, here, at the place where the personal identity card had been lost. I think that you were asking me who was in charge of issuing him with a duplicate card. What it says, here, is what the obligation of every citizen is, to report to the closest police station the loss of any form of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says "any form of identification"? I thought this was referring just specifically to the personal identification card. Isn't that a unique document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A personal identity card is a document that is used for identification; however, I've already said that citizens also have travel documents. Also, if a citizen loses a travel document, he is duty-bound to report the loss of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But not according to this decree. This decree only refers to the personal identification card, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, only personal identity cards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to finish in the next minute. I don't know if we could break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thirty minutes probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you finished with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you finish with that? There's no pressure today because there's no other case coming in here, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we could finish with one document, it would make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try and ask a couple more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard evidence from a number of Kosovo Albanian civilians about being directed to leave Kosovo and who indicated that as they were passing through the border at Albania on the way sometimes their identity cards and other personal documents were taken from them and torn up. As a practical matter, sir, can you tell me how a person whose card is torn up by a policeman could reasonably be expected to report that loss to the police station in the area where it happened? That's not realistic, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN VUCUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the citizen would be duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions about this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The article we're looking at obviously changes the rule in some way. What is the change that was made by Article 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that what was changed here was only the time. I don't have the Law on Personal Identity Cards here on me now, so the period within which one has to report the loss. I think that the law gives a general wording, as in immediately; whereas, here it says 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at Article 2, you'll see another change that anyone over 14 was obliged to have a personal identification card, and I think other evidence indicates that the previous age was 16. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The law says that every citizen who is of age is duty-bound to have a personal identity card. In our country, persons become of at age at the age of 18. Persons younger than 18 may have a personal identity card but need not necessarily have one. This is a change in relation to the law. This stipulates an obligation; whereas, the law provides for the possibility of younger persons having a personal identity card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know why this change was made during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't understand why this change was made, especially for persons who are younger than 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That brings the proceedings for today to an end, Mr. Vucurevic, which means you'll have to come back again tomorrow. Tomorrow that will be at 9.00 and will be in court 3 in this building. Please remember what I said to you about not having communications with anyone about the evidence in the case while you're a witness. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24
